steps.text: Part 4 of 4: Double check: how to see it, set it up and stop it. This part covers A real example; Say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.prompt: Before the answer: name the checks White has, then the one you would test first.

steps.text: **A real position.** A famous double check was played by Réti against Tartakower, Vienna 1910 [R]; our famous-game lesson shows the whole game. This position is from an online game (Lichess puzzle database, CC0). Do not hunt for moves yet. List every check White has, then ask which of them has a piece behind it.

steps.prompt: Teach a beginner. Write four things: what a double check is, when it works, an example they could set up on a board (pieces and squares), and one warning. Self-check, nothing is graded: did you say why only the king can answer, name one condition that can fail, and give a look-alike?

steps.caption: White to move. The queen on b3 aims along a diagonal at the king on g8, and White's rook on e6 stands on it.

line.say: The rook checks along the eighth rank and uncovers the queen's check: two checks.
The king has one legal move.
The queen lands on g8, protected by the rook: checkmate.

claims.statement: After the rook moves, two white pieces attack the king.
White forces mate within two moves.
This move is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.caption: The tempting alternative. Taking the black queen also gives check.

line.say: The rook takes the queen and uncovers the queen's check. But the rook on g6 gives no check itself: a single check.
Black takes the checking queen with the rook. A double check would have allowed no such answer.
White recaptures. Queens are off and the attack is gone.

claims.statement: After the capture, only one white piece attacks the king on g8.
The capture is at least six pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **What others say.** Nimzowitsch (*My System*, chapter on discovered check) describes double check as leaving the king nothing but flight, and calls it purely tactical [V-sheet: paraphrased from our own notes, not the book page]. Jacob Aagaard argues that many calculation errors start with a candidate move that was never considered [S, a reviewer's account, paraphrased]. [I] So the habit: put the double check on your candidate list before you calculate.

**What to remember.**
1. Double check: two checkers, so only the king can move.
2. A back piece, a front piece, an open line.
3. The front piece must check from where it lands.
4. The king may take a checker next to it, if nothing covers that square.
5. Count the flight squares: mate, or a free move.
6. Look-alikes: blocked line, or no front check.
7. Defence: ask what long-range piece stands behind a piece that could check you. Move the king or either piece.

steps.prompt: A model answer [I], in the author's words. Idea: one move makes two pieces check at once, so only the king can answer. When it works: the line is open, the front piece checks where it lands, and the king cannot take the checker or reach a safe square. Example: White rook e1, bishop e5, pawn c5, Black king e7; the bishop to d6 is mate. Warning: without the pawn on c5 the king takes the bishop. Compare with yours.

steps.text: **Remember.** A double check means one move makes two pieces give check, so only the king can move. List every check before you calculate, and ask which one has a piece behind it. It fails if the king can take a checker or has a safe square.
